tips.title: Derive the lens, never recall it
tips.body: Ask **where the image forms**. In **front** of the retina → push it **back** → **spread** the light → **concave**. **Behind** → pull it **forward** → **converge** the light → **convex**. Two steps, and it cannot come out backwards.

tips.title: Concave caves in
tips.body: A **concave** lens **caves in** at the middle, so it is thinner there and **spreads light out**. A **convex** lens bulges, so it is thicker in the middle and **brings light together**. The shape tells you what it does.

tips.title: The iris is the muscle, the pupil the hole
tips.body: The pupil does not contract; it **gets smaller because the circular muscles of the iris contract**. Where marks are tight, name the muscle — and remember the radial muscles do the opposite job.

tips.title: Three kinds of problem, not four defects
tips.body: **Focusing** (short and long sight) — a lens moves the image. **Transmission** (cataract) — the light is scattered, so surgery. **Detection** (colour blindness) — the cones fail, so nothing optical helps. *Why can glasses not fix this* is testing that.

tips.title: Rods for dim, cones for colour
tips.body: **Rod** cells work in **dim** light and see **no colour**; **cone** cells need **bright** light and **do** see colour. That single pair of facts explains why a moonlit garden is grey — the light still has its colour, but your cones cannot report it.

why.matters:
An eye has to do two things a camera also does — let in the right amount of light, and focus it — and it has to do the second one **continuously**, because what you look at keeps changing distance.

Both jobs are done by muscles changing a shape: the iris changes the size of the pupil, and the ciliary muscles change the shape of the lens. Once you can say which muscle does which, the defects and their corrections follow without being learned separately.

examples.title: Why your eyes hurt coming out of a cinema
examples.body:
In the dark the **radial** muscles of the iris contract and the pupil opens wide, letting in as much light as possible. Step outside and there is far too much of it arriving at a retina set up for the dark.

The **circular** muscles then contract and the pupil closes down within a second, and the retina itself takes longer to adjust; until both have, the light is too much. It is a reflex — automatic, no thinking — which is also why you cannot decide to widen your own pupils, and why a torch in the eye is what a paramedic uses to check the reflex is working.

visual.alt: A table of the pupil reflex: in dim light the radial muscles contract and the circular ones relax so the pupil widens, and in bright light the opposite happens and it narrows

examples.title: Why reading tires your eyes and looking at hills does not
examples.body:
Focusing on something distant is the eye's resting state: the ciliary muscles are **relaxed**, the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight, and the lens is stretched thin.

Close work is the opposite. The ciliary muscles **contract**, the ligaments slacken, and the lens becomes fatter so it refracts more strongly. That is muscular work, held for as long as you keep reading — which is why looking up at something far away every so often genuinely rests your eyes, and why *staring into the distance* is not the effort it sounds like.

visual.alt: A table of accommodation: for a near object the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments slacken and the lens becomes fatter, while for a distant one the muscles relax, the ligaments pull tight and the lens is thin

examples.title: Why the two kinds of glasses are opposite shapes
examples.body:
Short sight means the eyeball is too long, or the lens refracts too strongly, so light from a distant object is brought to a focus **in front of** the retina. The correction has to spread the light out a little first, which is a **concave** lens.

Long sight is the reverse: light from something close would come to a focus **behind** the retina, so it needs help converging, which is a **convex** lens. Once you know where the image lands, the lens follows — and the same reasoning explains why reading glasses are thicker in the middle.

steps.title: How the eye focuses light
steps.body:
This whole topic is **Biology only** (2.15B to 2.17B).

The eye is a **sensory receptor**: it detects light and converts it into electrical impulses for the nervous system. The specification names three parts and what each does.

**The cornea and the lens** both **refract** — bend — the light, focusing it onto the **retina** at the back of the eye.

- The **cornea** is the transparent front of the eye. It does **most** of the bending, but its shape is fixed, so it cannot adjust.
- The **lens** does the **fine adjustment**. It changes shape to focus on objects at different distances, which is called **accommodation**.

That division of labour is worth knowing: the cornea provides most of the focusing power and the lens provides the **adjustable** part.

**The iris** is the coloured ring, and it controls the **size of the pupil** — the hole in its middle — and so how much light enters:

- In **bright** light the pupil **constricts** (gets smaller), so less light enters and the retina is protected.
- In **dim** light the pupil **dilates** (gets larger), so more light enters and you can see.

This is a **reflex**, so it happens automatically and quickly.

A point of precision: the **iris** is the muscle; the **pupil** is the hole. The pupil does not do anything — it is changed in size by the iris.

steps.title: Rod and cone cells
steps.body:
The **retina** contains two kinds of light-sensitive cell, and the difference between them explains a great deal about how vision behaves.

**Rod cells:**

- work in **dim** light
- do **not** detect colour
- are found across most of the retina

**Cone cells:**

- need **bright** light
- **do** detect colour, in three types sensitive to red, green and blue light
- are concentrated at the centre of the retina

This is why you see **no colour in near darkness**: only the rods are working, and rods cannot tell one colour from another. Look at a garden by moonlight and it is all greys — not because the light has lost its colour, but because your cone cells have too little light to respond.

It also explains why something faint is easier to see when you look slightly to one side of it: you are placing its image away from the cone-rich centre and onto the rods, which are more sensitive in dim light.

**Colour blindness** is a defect of the **cone cells** — usually one type not working properly, most often those for red or green. It is a fault in the **detection** of light, not in its focusing, which is why glasses cannot correct it.

steps.title: Short-sightedness and long-sightedness
steps.body:
Both defects are the same kind of problem: the image does **not** form on the retina. What differs is **where** it forms instead — and the lens that corrects it follows directly from that.

The same corrections can also be made with **contact lenses**, or by **laser surgery** that reshapes the cornea so that it refracts the light by the right amount.

steps.title: Cataracts
steps.body:
A **cataract** is a different kind of defect. The **lens becomes cloudy**, so light cannot pass through it clearly.

The effects follow from that:

- Vision becomes **blurred** or misty.
- **Colours look faded**, because less light reaches the cone cells.
- There is often **glare** around bright lights, as the cloudy lens scatters the light.

Cataracts are most common in older people, and are made more likely by long exposure to **ultraviolet light**, by smoking, and by diabetes.

**The correction is not a lens.** Glasses cannot **correct** it. Stronger glasses may help a little early on, but no lens can clear the cloudiness, because the light is being **scattered** on the way through, not focused in the wrong place. The treatment is **surgery**: the cloudy lens is **removed and replaced with an artificial one**.

That contrast is worth holding on to, because it is what the three defects together are testing:

- **Short and long sight** are **focusing** problems — the image is sharp but in the wrong place. A **lens** moves it.
- **A cataract** is a **transmission** problem — the light never gets through cleanly. **Surgery** replaces the lens.
- **Colour blindness** is a **detection** problem — the light arrives and is focused correctly, but the cone cells do not respond properly. Neither lenses nor surgery corrects it.

steps.title: The pupil reflex
steps.body:
The change in pupil size is a **reflex**, which connects this topic to the reflex arc.

**In bright light:**

- Light is detected by receptors in the **retina**.
- An impulse travels to the **CNS**.
- The **circular muscles** of the iris **contract** and the radial muscles relax.
- The **pupil constricts** — gets smaller.
- **Less light enters**, protecting the retina from damage.

**In dim light** everything reverses: the **radial muscles contract**, the circular ones relax, the **pupil dilates**, and **more light enters** so that more can be seen.

**Why it is a reflex.** It is automatic and rapid, and it **protects the body** — in this case the retina, which bright light can damage. You cannot choose to keep your pupils wide in sunlight, which is exactly what makes it a reflex rather than a decision.

It is also a good example of two sets of muscles working **antagonistically** — in opposite directions — so that one contracting while the other relaxes moves the structure one way, and the reverse moves it back.

steps.title: Going deeper: working the lenses out
steps.body:
**Never memorise which lens goes with which defect.** Derive it, in two steps:

1. **Where is the image forming?** In **front** of the retina, or **behind** it?
2. **Which way must it move**, and what does that lens do?

- Image **in front** (short sight) → it must move **back** → the light must be **spread out** first → a **concave** lens.
- Image **behind** (long sight) → it must move **forward** → the light must be **brought together** sooner → a **convex** lens.

Done that way you cannot get it the wrong way round, and it still works if a question phrases the defect unusually.

A memory aid for the lens shapes themselves: a **concave** lens **caves in** at the middle, so it is thinner there and spreads light out. A **convex** lens bulges out, so it is thicker in the middle and brings light together.

**Three different kinds of problem.** The four defects on the specification are not four versions of one thing, and noticing that is what a top answer does:

- **Focusing**: short and long sight. The image is **sharp but in the wrong place**, so moving it with a **lens** fixes it.
- **Transmission**: a cataract. The light is **scattered on the way in**, so no lens can correct it — the cloudy lens is **replaced surgically**.
- **Detection**: colour blindness. The image arrives correctly focused, but the **cone cells** do not respond. Nothing optical corrects it, because nothing optical is wrong.

A question asking *why can glasses not correct this* is asking whether you have understood that distinction.

**Why no colour in the dark.** Only **cone** cells detect colour, and cones need **bright** light. In dim light only the **rods** respond, and rods cannot distinguish colours — so the scene appears in shades of grey. The light still carries the colour; your retina simply cannot report it.

**One precision to keep.** The **iris** is the muscle and the **pupil** is the hole. Writing *the pupil contracts* is loose — the pupil gets smaller because the **circular muscles of the iris contract**. Where the marks are tight, name the muscle.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The eye is a **sensory receptor**: it detects light and produces electrical impulses.
- The **cornea** and the **lens** both **refract** light onto the **retina**. The cornea does most of the focusing; the **lens adjusts** to different distances.
- The **iris** is the coloured **muscle** controlling the size of the **pupil**, which is the **hole**.
- **Bright** light: the pupil **constricts**, protecting the retina. **Dim** light: it **dilates**, letting more light in. This is a **reflex**.
- **Rod cells** work in **dim** light and do **not** detect colour.
- **Cone cells** need **bright** light and **do** detect colour, in three types.
- There is **no colour in near darkness** because only the rods are working.
- **Short-sightedness**: the image forms **in front of** the retina; corrected with a **concave** lens, which **spreads light out**.
- **Long-sightedness**: the image forms **behind** the retina; corrected with a **convex** lens, which **brings light together**.
- **Cataract**: the **lens becomes cloudy** and scatters light. Corrected by **surgery**, not glasses.
- **Colour blindness**: the **cone cells** do not respond properly. Not correctable by lenses or surgery.
- Work the lens out from **where the image forms**, rather than memorising which is which.

questions.prompt: Explain what happens in a short-sighted eye and in a long-sighted eye, and explain how each defect is corrected.
questions.solution: In a short sighted eye, distant objects appear blurred while near objects can be seen clearly. This happens because the light is brought to a focus in front of the retina rather than on it, either because the eyeball is too long or because the lens is too strong. To correct this the light must be made to come to a focus further back, so a concave lens is used. A concave lens spreads the light out before it enters the eye, so that the eye's own focusing brings it to a point further back, on the retina. In a long sighted eye the opposite is true: near objects appear blurred while distant objects can be seen clearly. Here the light would come to a focus behind the retina, either because the eyeball is too short or because the lens is too weak. To correct this the light must be brought together sooner, so a convex lens is used. A convex lens brings the light together before it enters the eye, adding the focusing power that the eye lacks, so that the image forms on the retina.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Short sight.** **Distant** objects are blurred; near ones are clear.

- The light comes to a focus **in front of** the retina.
- Because the eyeball is **too long**, or the lens **too strong**.
- The image must move **back**, so the light must be **spread out** first.
- A **concave** lens does that — it spreads the light before it enters, so the eye's own focusing brings it to a point further back, on the retina.

**Long sight.** **Near** objects are blurred; distant ones are clear.

- The light would come to a focus **behind** the retina.
- Because the eyeball is **too short**, or the lens **too weak**.
- The image must move **forward**, so the light must be **brought together sooner**.
- A **convex** lens does that, adding the focusing power the eye lacks.

**Do not memorise which lens is which.** Ask where the image is forming and which way it must move. Concave **caves in**, so it spreads light out; convex bulges, so it brings light together. Derived that way, it cannot come out backwards.

questions.prompt: A person has cataracts and a second person is colour blind. Explain what is wrong in each case, and explain why neither can be corrected with glasses.
questions.solution: In a person with cataracts the lens of the eye has become cloudy. Light is scattered as it passes through the cloudy lens, so vision becomes blurred, colours appear faded and there is often glare around bright lights. Glasses cannot correct this because a lens in front of the eye works by changing where the light is brought to a focus. In short sightedness and long sightedness the image is sharp but is formed in the wrong place, so moving it with a lens solves the problem. In a cataract the image is blurred by scattering as the light passes through the cloudy lens, so moving it with a lens does not fix it. Stronger glasses may help a little early on, but they cannot correct it. The treatment is surgery, in which the cloudy lens is removed and replaced with an artificial one. In a person who is colour blind the cone cells of the retina do not respond properly, usually because one type of cone, most often the red or green type, is not working. The light entering the eye is focused perfectly well onto the retina, so the problem is not one of focusing at all but of detection. Since nothing optical is wrong, no lens can correct it.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Cataracts.** The **lens has become cloudy**. Light is **scattered** as it passes through, so vision is blurred, colours look faded, and bright lights produce glare.

**Why glasses cannot correct it.** A corrective lens works by **changing where the light is brought to a focus**. In short or long sight the image is **sharp but in the wrong place**, so moving it solves the problem. In a cataract the image is **blurred by scattering**, so moving it does not fix it.

The treatment is **surgery**: the cloudy lens is removed and replaced with an artificial one.

**Colour blindness.** The **cone cells** of the retina do not respond properly — usually one type, most often red or green, is not working.

**Why glasses cannot correct it.** The light is **focused perfectly well** onto the retina. The problem is not **focusing** but **detection**, and since nothing optical is wrong, nothing optical can correct it.

The two cases together make the general point: the four defects on the specification are **three different kinds of problem** — focusing, transmission and detection — and the treatment follows from which kind it is.

questions.prompt: Light from a small object falls on the exact point of the retina where the optic nerve leaves the eye. Why can the person not see the object?
questions.skill: the retina and the optic nerve
questions.solution: **No receptors there.** The retina detects light with its **rod and cone cells**, which send impulses along the **optic nerve** to the brain. At the point where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no rods or cones, so light landing there produces no impulses and nothing is seen: this is the blind spot. The optic nerve does not reflect light; the lens focuses light across the whole retina; and impulses in the optic nerve only ever travel towards the brain.

Looking to one side makes the pupil dilate further, so that enough extra light enters for the cone cells at the centre of the retina to respond
Looking to one side makes the lens change shape, so that the star's light is brought to a much sharper focus on the centre of the retina

questions.prompt: In a short-sighted eye, light from a distant object is brought to a focus in front of the retina. Laser surgery corrects the defect by reshaping the cornea. Which change to the cornea corrects it?
questions.skill: correcting short-sightedness by reshaping the cornea
questions.solution: **Flatten it.** Work from where the image forms: in front of the retina means the light is being bent too much, so the image must move back, so the eye must refract less. The cornea does most of the eye's refraction, and a flatter cornea bends light less, which is exactly what a concave lens in a pair of glasses does from outside the eye. A more curved cornea would bend the light more and move the image further forward; a cloudy cornea would scatter light, as a cataract does, and blur everything; and how long light takes to pass through has nothing to do with focusing.

markScheme.description: flattening it, so it refracts less and the image moves back onto the retina

options: Making it more curved, so that it refracts the light more and the image moves back onto the retina
Flattening it, so that it refracts the light less and the image moves back onto the retina
Making it slightly cloudy, so that it scatters the light and spreads the image across the whole retina
Making it thicker, so that light takes longer to pass through it and the lens has more time to adjust

questions.prompt: Name the process by which the lens of the eye changes shape to focus on objects at different distances.
questions.solution: **Accommodation.** The cornea does most of the eye's refraction but its shape is fixed; the lens provides the fine adjustment, changing shape so that light from a near object or a distant one is focused on the retina.

markScheme.description: accommodation

questions.prompt: In a fictional survey, 2 500 boys and 2 500 girls were tested for red-green colour blindness. 200 of the boys and 10 of the girls were found to be colour blind. Calculate the percentage of the boys who were colour blind.
questions.solution: $\dfrac{200}{2\,500} \times 100 = 8\%$ of the boys. For the girls it would be $\dfrac{10}{2\,500} \times 100 = 0.4\%$, so in this survey the defect was 20 times as common in boys. Colour blindness is a fault in the cone cells of the retina, usually one type not working properly, so it is a problem of detecting light, not of focusing it, and no lens corrects it.

markScheme.description: divides 200 by 2 500 and multiplies by 100

questions.prompt: In dim light a person's pupil is 8 mm in diameter. In bright light the muscles of the iris constrict it to 2 mm in diameter. The amount of light entering the eye is proportional to the area of the pupil, where area $= \pi r^2$. Calculate how many times more light enters the eye through the 8 mm pupil than through the 2 mm pupil.
questions.skill: pupil area and the light entering the eye
questions.solution: Radius first, not diameter: 4 mm and 1 mm. Areas: $\pi \times 4^2 = 16\pi$, about 50.3 mm², and $\pi \times 1^2 = \pi$, about 3.14 mm². Ratio $= \dfrac{16\pi}{\pi} = 16$. So 16 times as much light enters through the wide pupil, not 4 times: the diameter is 4 times larger, and the area grows with the square of that. This is why the pupil reflex protects the retina so effectively; constricting the pupil in bright light cuts the light reaching the rods and cones by a factor of 16.

markScheme.description: uses the radii 4 mm and 1 mm to find the areas, 16π and π (about 50.3 and 3.14 mm²)
divides the larger area by the smaller

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of the cornea and the lens in forming a focused image on the retina.
questions.solution: Both the cornea and the lens **refract** light, bending it so that rays from an object are brought together to a focus on the **retina**. The **cornea**, the transparent front of the eye, does **most** of the refraction, but its shape is fixed so it cannot adjust. The **lens** provides the **fine adjustment**: it changes shape, becoming fatter for near objects and thinner for distant ones, so that objects at different distances can each be focused on the retina. This adjustment is called accommodation.

markScheme.description: both refract (bend) light to focus it on the retina
the cornea does most of the refraction but has a fixed shape
the lens changes shape to focus objects at different distances (accommodation)

criteria.text: Says that both the cornea and the lens refract (bend) light so that it is focused on the retina
Says that the cornea does most of the refraction but its shape is fixed, so it cannot adjust
Says that the lens changes shape to focus objects at different distances, which is accommodation

questions.modelAnswer: Light entering the eye has to be bent so that the rays from each point of an object meet at a single point on the retina, and two structures do the bending. The cornea is the transparent front of the eye, and because light passes from air into it, it refracts the light strongly; it provides most of the eye's focusing power. Its shape is fixed, however, so it bends every ray by the same amount whatever the distance of the object. The lens behind it provides the fine adjustment. It is held by muscles that can change its shape: for a near object it becomes fatter and refracts the light more, and for a distant object it becomes thinner and refracts it less. This changing of the lens's shape to keep the image on the retina as the distance changes is called accommodation. Together the fixed cornea and the adjustable lens bring light to a sharp focus on the retina, where the rod and cone cells detect it.

questions.prompt: During an eye examination, drops are put into a patient's eyes that stop the circular muscles of the iris from contracting for several hours. The patient is told to wear dark glasses outdoors until the drops wear off. Explain why.
questions.skill: the iris and protecting the retina
questions.solution: In bright light, receptors in the retina send impulses to the central nervous system and, by reflex, the **circular muscles** of the iris **contract** while the radial muscles relax, so the pupil **constricts** and less light enters. With the circular muscles unable to contract, the pupil stays wide and this **reflex cannot happen**. Outdoors, far **too much light** enters the eye, and bright light can **damage the retina**, the rod and cone cells that detect it. Dark glasses reduce the light reaching the eye, doing from outside what the iris cannot do for the time being.

markScheme.description: normally the circular muscles contract (and the radial muscles relax) in bright light so the pupil constricts: the pupil reflex
with them unable to contract the pupil cannot constrict, so too much light enters the eye outdoors
bright light can damage the retina (the rods and cones), so dark glasses cut the light instead

criteria.text: Explains that in bright light the circular muscles of the iris normally contract, and the radial muscles relax, so the pupil constricts: this is the pupil reflex
Explains that with the circular muscles unable to contract, the pupil cannot constrict, so far too much light enters the eye outdoors
Explains that bright light can damage the retina (the rod and cone cells), so the dark glasses reduce the light entering instead

questions.modelAnswer: The size of the pupil is controlled by the iris, and the change is a reflex. In bright light, receptors in the retina detect the light and send impulses to the central nervous system, which sends impulses back to the iris: the circular muscles contract and the radial muscles relax, so the pupil constricts and less light enters the eye. The drops stop the circular muscles from contracting, so this reflex cannot happen. The pupil stays wide, as it would in a dark room, even in full daylight. Outdoors, far more light than normal reaches the back of the eye, and bright light can damage the retina, the layer of rod and cone cells that detect the light. The dark glasses do from outside what the iris cannot do for the moment: they cut down the light entering the eye and protect the retina until the drops wear off and the reflex works again. The patient will also find bright light uncomfortable and dazzling, which is the same reflex failing to protect them.

questions.prompt: The eye is a sensory receptor. Explain how light entering the eye is focused and converted into impulses that reach the brain, and explain why a garden seen by moonlight appears only in shades of grey.
questions.skill: the eye as a sensory receptor
questions.solution: Light is **refracted** first by the **cornea**, which does most of the focusing, and then by the **lens**, which changes shape to focus objects at different distances onto the retina: **accommodation**. The **iris** controls the size of the pupil; in moonlight the pupil **dilates** so that as much light as possible gets in. The **retina** holds the receptor cells, **rods and cones**, which detect the light and **convert it into electrical impulses** that pass along sensory neurones, the optic nerve, to the brain. **Cone cells** detect colour, in three types sensitive to red, green and blue light, but they need **bright** light; **rod cells** work in **dim** light but cannot tell one colour from another. By moonlight there is too little light for the cones, so only the rods respond, and a scene seen with rods alone is in shades of grey. The light still carries colour; the retina cannot detect it.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): names parts of the eye with their jobs, such as the lens focusing light or rods working in dim light, without linking them into a sequence

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes the cornea and lens refracting light onto the retina and the rods and cones producing impulses, and states that rods work in dim light while cones detect colour, but the explanation of grey vision or of accommodation is incomplete

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a full account: the cornea refracts most, the lens adjusts by changing shape, the iris dilates the pupil in dim light, rods and cones convert light to electrical impulses carried along sensory neurones to the brain, and only the rods, which cannot distinguish colour, respond in moonlight, so the colour is in the light but is not detected

criteria.text: Says that the cornea refracts (bends) the light and does most of the focusing
Says that the lens refracts the light further and changes shape (accommodation) so that objects at different distances are focused on the retina
Says that the iris controls the size of the pupil, and that in moonlight the pupil dilates so that as much light as possible enters
Says that rod and cone cells in the retina detect the light and convert it into electrical impulses, which pass along sensory neurones (the optic nerve) to the brain
Says that cone cells detect colour, in three types, but need bright light, while rod cells work in dim light but cannot distinguish colours
Explains that in moonlight only the rods respond, so the garden appears in shades of grey: the light still carries colour, but the retina cannot detect it

questions.modelAnswer:
**Focusing the light.** Light from the garden enters through the **cornea**, the transparent front of the eye. Passing from air into the cornea refracts the light strongly, and the cornea does most of the eye's focusing; its shape is fixed, so it bends every ray by the same amount. Behind the pupil the **lens** refracts the light further and provides the adjustment. Muscles change its shape, making it fatter for near objects and thinner for distant ones, so that whatever the person looks at is focused on the retina. This is **accommodation**. Between the two sits the **iris**, the coloured ring of muscle, which controls the size of the pupil, the hole in its middle. In bright light the pupil constricts to protect the retina; by moonlight the radial muscles contract and the pupil **dilates**, letting in as much of the little available light as possible.

**Converting light into impulses.** The focused image falls on the **retina**, the layer of light-sensitive cells at the back of the eye, and this is what makes the eye a sensory receptor. The **rod and cone cells** detect the light and convert it into **electrical impulses**. These pass along sensory neurones, bundled together as the optic nerve, to the brain, where the cerebral hemispheres interpret them as the scene being looked at.

**Two kinds of receptor cell.** **Cone cells** come in three types, sensitive to red, green and blue light; the brain compares the responses of the three and that comparison is colour vision. But cones need **bright** light to respond at all, and they are concentrated at the centre of the retina. **Rod cells** are spread across the rest of the retina and work in **dim** light, but there is only one kind of rod, so a rod can report how much light there is and nothing about its colour.

**Why the garden is grey.** Moonlight is far too dim for the cone cells, so they send no impulses, and the whole scene is reported by the rods alone. Rods cannot tell one colour from another, so the brain receives information only about brightness: the lawn, the flowers and the fence all appear as shades of grey. The light itself is not colourless, and the flowers have not changed. The colour is still in the light reaching the eye; by moonlight the retina simply has no working cells that can detect it.

examTechnique.body:
For a focusing defect, say where the image forms before naming the lens. The position is a mark of its own and it also tells you which lens to name.

Say what the correcting lens does, not just its name: a concave lens spreads light out, a convex lens brings it together.

Distinguish the iris from the pupil, and name the circular or radial muscles where the question is about the reflex.

For rod and cone cells, give both the light level and the colour, because the two together are what the comparison is for.

When asked why glasses cannot correct something, explain what a lens actually does and then why that does not apply.

Give causes as alternatives where the specification does: an eyeball too long or a lens too strong.
examinerErrors: Naming a convex lens for short-sightedness, or a concave lens for long-sightedness.
Saying the pupil contracts rather than the iris muscles contracting.
Saying a cataract is a problem with the retina.
Saying glasses can correct colour blindness.
Describing where the image forms without saying relative to the retina.
Saying the lens does most of the focusing, when the cornea does.
Saying colour blindness means seeing only in black and white.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer never recalls which lens goes with which defect: it states where the image forms, works out which way it must move, and names the lens from what that lens does. It treats the four defects as **three kinds of problem** — focusing, transmission and detection — so a question about why glasses cannot correct a defect is straightforward rather than a guess. It is precise about the iris and the pupil, and about the circular and radial muscles. And it can explain the absence of colour in darkness from the properties of rods and cones rather than as a separate fact to remember.
